q001.answer: Breadth-first search is a search that expands the frontier in order of depth; it is used because it guarantees the shallowest goal when every step costs the same.

q002.answer: A common mistake with depth-first search: assuming it will find a short path.

q003.answer: Uniform-cost search in practice: route planning where some roads are slower than others.

q004.answer: A* search is a best-first search ordered by cost so far plus an admissible heuristic; it is used because it is optimal and expands fewer nodes than uniform cost.

q005.answer: A common mistake with a heuristic function: confusing admissibility with consistency.

q006.answer: An admissible heuristic in practice: straight-line distance for road routing.

q007.answer: A consistent heuristic is a heuristic satisfying the triangle inequality on every edge; it is used because consistency keeps A* optimal even when it ignores re-expansions.

q008.answer: A common mistake with iterative deepening: repeating work without accounting for its cost.

q009.answer: Bidirectional search in practice: route planning between two known coordinates.

q010.answer: A constraint satisfaction problem is a set of variables, their domains, and the constraints between them; it is used because constraints prune the space before search touches it.

q011.answer: A common mistake with backtracking search: choosing the next variable in an arbitrary order.

q012.answer: Forward checking in practice: scheduling with tight resource constraints.

q013.answer: The AC-3 algorithm is an arc-consistency algorithm that propagates domain reductions to a queue; it is used because it shrinks domains before search begins.

q014.answer: A common mistake with the minimax algorithm: forgetting that the guarantee is only as good as the evaluation function.

q015.answer: Alpha-beta pruning in practice: any competitive game-playing engine.

q016.answer: Expectimax is a search that averages over outcomes of chance nodes; it is used because it handles dice and randomness without an adversarial assumption.

q017.answer: A common mistake with Monte Carlo tree search: believing it needs no evaluation function at all.

q018.answer: A Markov decision process in practice: inventory control under stochastic demand.

q019.answer: The Bellman equation is a recursive relationship between the value of a state and its successors; it is used because it turns a planning problem into an equation that can be solved iteratively.

q020.answer: A common mistake with value iteration: stopping when values look stable rather than measuring the residual.

q021.answer: Policy iteration in practice: control problems with few states.

q022.answer: The discount factor is a multiplier on future rewards; it is used because it makes an infinite-horizon sum finite and encodes time preference.

q023.answer: A common mistake with Q-learning: believing it works well with a fixed unvisited-state policy.

q024.answer: Temporal-difference learning in practice: value prediction from a stream of observations.

q025.answer: SARSA is an on-policy temporal-difference control method; it is used because it learns the value of the policy actually being followed.

q026.answer: A common mistake with the exploration-exploitation trade-off: annealing epsilon to zero too early.

q027.answer: Experience replay in practice: training a value function from a long log.

q028.answer: Policy gradient methods is methods that adjust the policy parameters directly in the direction of higher expected return; it is used because they handle continuous actions naturally.

q029.answer: A common mistake with proximal policy optimisation: ignoring the clipping range's effect on learning speed.

q030.answer: Deep Q-networks in practice: learning from pixels.

q031.answer: A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph of variables with conditional probability tables; it is used because it states the independence assumptions explicitly.

q032.answer: A common mistake with d-separation: forgetting that conditioning on a collider creates dependence.

q033.answer: Inference by enumeration in practice: a five-node network in a textbook exercise.

q034.answer: Variable elimination is summing out variables one at a time while multiplying factors; it is used because it avoids recomputing shared subexpressions.

q035.answer: A common mistake with rejection sampling: using it when the evidence is unlikely.

q036.answer: Likelihood weighting in practice: inference with strong evidence.

q037.answer: A hidden Markov model is a chain of hidden states with observations that depend on each state; it is used because it models a sequence with uncertainty about what generated it.

q038.answer: A common mistake with the forward algorithm: forgetting to normalise at each step.

q039.answer: Particle filtering in practice: tracking with a non-Gaussian belief.

q040.answer: Supervised machine learning is fitting a function from inputs to labels using examples; it is used because it generalises to inputs it has not seen.

q041.answer: A common mistake with generalisation: assuming the test set is representative.

q042.answer: A baseline in practice: predicting the majority class.

q043.answer: Overfitting is fitting noise in the training data rather than the signal; it is used because recognising it tells you whether regularisation is needed.

q044.answer: A common mistake with regularisation: tuning the strength on the test set.

q045.answer: Cross-validation in practice: choosing a hyperparameter with little data.

q046.answer: Calibration is agreement between predicted probabilities and observed frequencies; it is used because a confident model that is wrong is worse than an uncertain one.

q047.answer: A common mistake with backpropagation: forgetting to zero the gradients between steps.

q048.answer: A convolutional network in practice: image classification.

q049.answer: Dropout is randomly zeroing activations during training; it is used because it discourages co-adaptation of features.

q050.answer: A common mistake with the transformer: forgetting that attention has no inherent notion of order.

q051.answer: Self-attention in practice: modelling long-range dependencies.

q052.answer: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is training a reward model on human comparisons, then optimising a policy against it; it is used because it aligns behaviour with preferences that are hard to write as a rule.

q053.answer: A common mistake with retrieval-augmented generation: measuring retrieval and generation separately and never together.

q054.answer: BM25 in practice: a first-pass retriever over a small corpus.

q055.answer: A dense retriever is a retriever that ranks by similarity in a learned vector space; it is used because it matches paraphrases that share no words.

q056.answer: A common mistake with recall at k: reporting mean reciprocal rank when recall is what matters.

q057.answer: Hallucination in practice: a system that cites a passage that does not contain the claim.

q058.answer: Algorithmic fairness is the study of how a model's errors and benefits distribute across groups; it is used because aggregate accuracy can hide harm to a subgroup.

q059.answer: A common mistake with differential privacy: treating a large epsilon as privacy.

q060.answer: A risk management framework in practice: assessing a model before deployment.

q061.answer: Robot localisation is estimating a robot's pose from noisy sensors and a map; it is used because a robot that knows where it is can plan.

q062.answer: A common mistake with perception: evaluating perception in isolation from the task.

q063.answer: Automated planning in practice: planning a delivery route that minimises total distance.
